description: One cup of bread flour weighs 120 grams, spooned and levelled. That is the same as all-purpose flour. Convert bread flour between cups and grams.

steps: Multiply by the weight of one cup: 2 × 120 g.
examples.title: 2 cups of bread flour to grams

steps: Divide by the weight of one cup: 180 ÷ 120.
examples.title: 180 g of bread flour to cups

faqs.answer: 120 grams, when the cup is spooned and levelled. That is the figure on King Arthur Baking's ingredient weight chart.
faqs.question: How many grams are in a cup of bread flour?

faqs.answer: Because cup weight depends on how the flour packs, not on its protein. Both are white wheat flours ground to a similar fineness, so a level cup of each holds 120 grams. The protein difference shows up in the dough, not on the scale.
faqs.question: Why does bread flour weigh the same as all-purpose flour?

faqs.answer: By weight, yes. A cup of one is 120 grams and a cup of the other is 120 grams, so the numbers stay the same. The texture changes, though. Bread flour gives a chewier crumb and a higher rise, so it suits bread better than cakes.
faqs.question: Can I swap bread flour for all-purpose flour?

faqs.answer: Just over 4 cups. 500 ÷ 120 = 4.17 cups, which is 4 cups plus about 2 1/2 tablespoons.
faqs.question: How many cups is 500 g of bread flour?

faqs.answer: Only if the recipe tells you to. Sifting makes flour lighter, so a sifted cup weighs less than 120 grams. '1 cup flour, sifted' means measure first, then sift. '1 cup sifted flour' means sift first, and the weight will be lower.
faqs.question: Should I sift bread flour before measuring?

felicityNote: I used to buy bread flour and all-purpose flour and treat them as different worlds. Same cup weight. The difference is in the chew, not the measuring cup.

parts.meaning: The volume in the recipe, measured spooned and levelled.
The grams in one cup of bread flour, from King Arthur Baking's chart.
The weight on the scale. It does not change with how you fill the cup.

howToSteps.name: Fluff the flour
howToSteps.text: Stir the flour in its bag or canister with a spoon a few times. Flour settles and packs down in storage, and fluffing it up is what makes the cup weigh 120 grams instead of 140.

howToSteps.name: Spoon it into the cup
howToSteps.text: Spoon the flour into the measuring cup until it heaps over the top. Do not scoop with the cup itself. Scooping packs the flour down.

howToSteps.name: Level it off
howToSteps.text: Sweep the flat edge of a knife across the rim of the cup, back into the bag. The cup is now level and holds one cup.

howToSteps.name: Convert or weigh
howToSteps.text: Weigh the flour if you have a scale: one level cup should read 120 grams. Or use the converter above. Cups times 120 is grams, grams divided by 120 is cups.

name: Bread Flour
sourceNote: King Arthur Baking lists bread flour at 120 g per cup (4 1/4 oz).
title: Bread Flour Cups to Grams Converter
tutorial: Here is the surprise: bread flour weighs exactly the same as all-purpose flour by the cup. One cup, spooned and levelled, is 120 grams. The flours differ in protein, not in cup weight. Bread flour has more protein, which is what builds the strong gluten network that makes bread chewy. But protein lives inside the flour particles. It does not change how much flour fits in a cup.

Measure it the same way as any flour. Fluff it up with a spoon first, spoon it into the cup until it heaps over the top, then sweep a knife across the rim. Never scoop with the cup. A scooped cup packs the flour down and can hold 140 grams or more, and that extra flour makes bread dense instead of open and springy.

The converter works in both directions. Cups become grams when you want the accuracy of the scale, which matters more in bread than anywhere else. Grams become cups when the recipe is in grams and the scale is nowhere to be found. Both directions use the same number: 120 grams per cup.

The halves are the anchor to remember. Half a cup is 60 grams, a quarter cup is 30 grams, two cups is 240 grams. Most bread recipes land on those numbers, and once they are in your head you barely need the converter at all.

One thing worth knowing: because the cup weight matches all-purpose flour, you can swap the two by weight without changing the numbers. The dough will still behave differently. Bread flour drinks a little more water and builds a chewier crumb. If a recipe calls for all-purpose flour and you use bread flour, expect a firmer bite, not a different weight.
